WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS 
IIT in Andhra Pradesh  
*1. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether his Ministry has considered the proposa l of Andhra 
Pradesh Government for establishment of an IIT at Basara in Adilabad district 
of Andhra Pradesh; 
.  (b) if so, the details of the proposal and the action taken thereon, 
indicating the amount sanctioned for this purpose; 
(c) whether, on the recommendation of an expert Committ ee constituted 
by Andhra Pradesh Government, the Union Government propose to upgrade 
Osmania University College of Engineering and Techn ology and Andhra 
Pradesh College of Engineering to IIT status; 
(d) if so, by when, and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (e) This Ministry had received  a proposal from the 
Government of Andhra Pradesh for the establishment of an Indian Institute of 
Technology (IIT) at Basara in Adilabad District of Andhra Pradesh. It was 
indicated in the proposal that the State Government had decided to allocate 1000 
acres of land along with civic amenities for the se tting up of an IIT at this 
place. Subsequently, a decision was taken to set up three new Indian Institutes 
of Technology (NTs) in the country. One of the thre e new IITs, is proposed to 
be set up in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The Minis ter of Human Resource 
Development vide his letter dated 16.12.2006, has requested the Chief Minister 
of Andhra Pradesh to provide free of cost 500 to 60 0 acres of land at a 
suitable location which should have the necessary p hysical and social 
infrastructure including good road, rail and air co nnectivity. The State 
Government has informed this Ministry that they are in the process of finalizing 
a suitable piece of land with good infrastructure facilities, for the setting up of 
an IIT in Andhra Pradesh. 
2 

[26 February, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
The Central Government, on the recommendation of an  Expert 
Committee which was constituted by the Government o f India, have 
identified seven institutions in the country which are proposed to be upgraded 
to the level of an NT. Osmania University College of Engineering and Technology, 
Hyderabad and Andhra Pradesh College of Engineering, Visakhapatnam, are 
amongst the seven institutions identified for this purpose. In order to upgrade 
the infrastructure to the level of IIT of the above  two institutions, Rs. 7.00 
crores to Osmania University College of Engineering  and Technology, 
Hyderabad and Rs. 8.00 crores to Andhra Pradesh Col lege of Engineering, 
Visakhapatnam, have been released during the current financial year 2006-07. 
Power generation by 2020  
*2. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government nave the capacity to generate 21 ,180 
Megawatts of electricity by 2020, under its calculated power programme; 
(b) whether the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) had a lso 
submitted certain proposals in this regard to the Committee of Secretaries in early 
December, 2006; and 
(c) if so, the number of proposals examined by the said  Committee and 
what is the outcome thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a ) 
Yes, Sir. The present nuclear power capacity of 390 0 MWe in the country is 
expected to increase to 7280 MWe by the end of Elev enth Plan on 
completion of projects already under construction. The Eleventh Plan 
proposals envisage commencement of work on 8x700 MW e of indigenous 
Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) totaling 5600 MWe capacity by 
Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. (NPCIL). Four Fast Breeder Reactors 
(FBRs) of 500 MWe each are planned to be executed by Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut 
Nigam Limited (BHAVINI Ltd.) by 2020. Thus, a capacity of about 15000 MWe 
is planned to be reached by 2020 only through indig enous efforts by the two 
Public Sector Undertakings under the administrative control of the Department 
of Atomic Energy (namely, NPCIL 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [26 February, 2007] 
and BHAVINI Ltd.) set up for this purpose. The effo rts of the Government to 
access imported reactors and fuel through internati onal cooperation would 
open up the possibility of further capacity addition reaching a capacity well beyond 
20,000 MWe by the year 2020. However, achieving suc h capacity addition by 
NPCIL will depend upon future developments in this regard. 
(b) Department of Atomic Energy have not submitted any proposal for 
setting up of neclear power plants for consideratio n of the Committee of 
Secretaries. 
(c) Does not arise. 
Begging by children 
†*3. DR. PRABHA THAKUR: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that thousands of children 
in the country are either engaged in begging or bei ng used as means of 
begging; 
(b) the steps taken by Government to protect them from such 
exploitation; 
(c) whether Government are aware that several anti-soci al 
organisations are engaged in these activities who torture these innocent children 
after kidnapping and make them source of their income by forcing them to beg; 
and 
(d) the measures taken by Government to salvage these t iny kids from 
such in-human and exploiting situation and whether these measures have proved 
to be effective; if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT 
(SHRIMATI MEIRA KUMAR): (a) to (d) Beggary is an in tricate problem 
having socio-cultural and economic ramifications. It is also a kind of wanton 
deviation on the part of those who beg willfully, habitually and professionally. Hence, 
it is a law & order problem also. The main action to prevent beggary lies with the 
State Government/Union Territories. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

Validity of laws placed in the Ninth Schedule of the                      
Constitution  
*4.     SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: 
SHRI AMAR SINGH: 
Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to review the Constitution of India in the 
wake of recent Supreme Court order which lays down that all laws placed in the 
Ninth Schedule after 1973 would be open to judicial review; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, in what manner Government propose to resolv e the 
reservation policy of Tamil Nadu Government which has made reservation to the 
extent of 69 per cent? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): 
(a) to (c) The Government is analysing the judgement of the Supreme Court in 
the matter of I.R. Coelho (Dead) By LRs V. State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. reported 
in JT 2007 (2) SC 292 and will take appropriate decision in the matter. 
Increase in the number of Anganwadis  
*5. SHRI K.E. ISMAIL: Will the Minister of WOMEN AN D CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Supreme Court has  ordered Government 
to take measures to increase the number of Anganwad is from the present 
six lakhs to fourteen lakhs in a phased manner by 2 008 in order to realize 
the commitment made in the Common Minimum Programme  of UPA 
Government to universalize the ICDS Scheme; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the measures bei ng taken by 
Government; 
(c) whether it is a fact that some State Governments ha ve failed to 
implement the earlier orders of the Supreme Court in this regard; and 
(d) if so, which are the States lagging behind in implementing the ICDS 
Scheme and what action is being taken against these States? 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [26 February, 2007] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and 
(b) Yes, Sir. The Supreme Court, vide its order dated 13.12.2006 in CWP No. 
196/2001-filed by People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) Vs.Union of India 
and Others, directed, inter-alia, the Union Government, to sanction and 
operationalise a minimum of 14 lakh Anganwadi Centres (AWCs) in a phased and 
even manner starting forthwith and ending December 2008. In doing so, the 
Central Government shall identify SC and ST hamlets / habitations for AWC 
on a priority basis. 
In pursuance of this direction and to fulfil the commitment enunciated in the 
National Common Minimum Programme of the Government, to have a functional 
Anganwadi Centre in every settlement/habitation, all the States/ UTs have been 
requested to furnish a list of un-covered habitations, along with population, which 
would require additional Anganwadi Centres (AWCs) Mini-AWCs in their States, 
In doing so they have also been requested to identi fy SC and SC 
hamlets/habitations for setting up AWCs and to ensure that no habitation/settlement 
with predominantly SC/ST Minority population is left out. 
In addition, to achieve Universalisation of ICDS the existing population norms 
are being revisited and further action for working out the requirement of additional 
ICDS projects/AWCs/Mini-AWCs to universalize the IC DS Scheme will be 
taken once the new population norms are in place. 
(c) and (d) As per the Supreme Court's order, 9 States/UTs namely, Bihar, 
Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Manipur, Punjab, West Bengal, Assam, Haryana and 
Uttar Pradesh are relatively lagging behind in the implementation of the ICDS 
Scheme. The Chief Secretaries of these States have specifically been directed to 
appear before the Court to explain why the orders requiring full implementation 
of the Scheme were not obeyed. 
The ICDS Scheme is a Centrally-sponsored scheme bei ng implemented 
through the States/UTs. To increase the effectiveness of the delivery of services 
udner ICDS in the country including the 9 identifie d States, following steps 
have been taken by the Government:- 
* All the States/UTs have been addressed by the Gov ernment to 
operationalise the recently sanctioned ICDS Projects and AWCs at the 
earliest. 
6 

[26 February, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
* To strengthen the existing monitoring and supervision mechanism for 
ICDS Scheme, the Government of India has set up of a Central 
Monitoring Unit (CMU) at National Institute of Public Cooperation and 
Child Development (NIPCCD) to monitor the Scheme th rough 
independent professional organization/institution i n each State/ UT. 
This is in addition to the monitoring mechanism in place at present. 
* A National Level Monitoring Committee has also been set up under the 
Chairpersonship of Minister of State for Women and Child 
Development (Independent Charge) to oversee the ent ire functioning 
of ICDS Scheme and to ensure that the services are delivered to the 
target groups in an effective manner and the object ives of the scheme 
are fulfilled within the overall framework of the ICDS Scheme.

Missing children in the country  
 *7.    SHRI K. CHANDRAN PILLAI: 
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the NHRC report lists nearly 45000 children going missing every 
year in the country; 
(b) whether according to the report, most children are reported missing from 
the State where the trafficking of children has become a highly profitable business; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that large number of miss ing children go 
untraced; 
(d) if so, the State-wise details to cases of missing c hildren for the last 
three years; 
(e) whether there is any mechanism to monitor the situation; and 
(f) the steps taken to protect the children? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a)T he 
NHRC in collaboration with the UNIFEM and the Institute of social Sciences, New 
Delhi conducted an Action Research on Trafficking in Women and Children in 
India (ARTWAC), the report of which was released in August, 2004. As per the 
report, the number of children reported missing from the 
10 

[26 February, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
State/Union Territories comes to an average of 44,476 per year based upon the 
data compiled for the six year period from 1996 to 2001.

Improvement in power distribution after privatisation 
†*8. SHRI JAI PARKASH AGGARWAL: Will the Minister of POWER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the qualitative improvements that have emerged in the field of power 
distribution as a result of its privatisation in the country; 
(b) whether any proposal is being considered by Governm ent regarding 
restructuring of power distribution model and to en courage lawful competition 
amongst existing power companies; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): ( a) 
The distribution of electricity has been privatized  in the National Capital 
Territory (NCT) of Delhi and in the State of Orissa. Under the Electricity Act, 
2003, the State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) have 
†Originai notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
12 

[26 February, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
been entrusted the function of specifying and enforcing the standards with respect 
to quality, continuity and reliability of services by licenses. 
The Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission (DERC) has informed the 
following: 
(i) The Aggregate Technical and Commercial Losses (AT&C) have come 
down from about 50% in 2002 (when the distribution system was 
privatised) to about 35% in March 2006 and the dist ribution 
companies (DISCOMS) have so far achieved the targets for loss 
reduction. 
(ii) At the time of privatisation, the Government of NCT of Delhi was 
spending about Rs.1200 crores every year on the ope ration of 
the Delhi Vidyut Board. This has since got substantially reduced 
and now, the Government of NCT of Delhi is only spe nding on 
the capital expenditure plans of the Generating Companies and the 
Delhi Transco Ltd. and for providing subsidy to cer tain groups 
of consumers in accordance with Section 65 of the E lectricity 
Act, 2003. 
In 2005-06, the Government of NCT of Delhi spent ab out Rs. 
91 crore for subsidising the power tariff for domes tic and 
agricultural consumers. This implies that additional funds are now 
available with the Government for other development schemes. 
(iii) Load shedding in Million Units (MU) has reduced from 558 MU 
in 2001-02 to about 321 MU in 2005-06. 
(iv) Distribution Transformer failure rate has reduced from 15% in 2002 
to less than 1.5% by the end of FY 2005-06. 
(v) Response time for attending to consumer complaints and for giving 
new connections has come down considerably. 
(vi) The available options for payment of electrici ty bills has 
increased manifold. 
Out of the four distribution companies in Orissa, the management of the 
Central Electricity Supply Company (CESCO) was vest ed in an 
Administrator appointed by the Orissa Electricity Regulatory Commission 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [26 February, 2007] 
(OERC) in the year 2001 consequent to the backing out of AES, the US based 
company. The performance of the distribution companies in Orissa during the 
financial year 2005-06 as made available by the OERC are as under: 
(i) All the Discoms have achieved the over all stan dard of 
performance fixed by OERC during financial year in respect of 
rectification of fuse-off calls in urban & rural areas except North 
Electricity Supply Company (NESCO). 
(ii) All the Discoms have achieved the overall stan dard of 
performance in restoration of line break downs. 
(iii) All discoms except NESCO have acieved the overall standard of 
performance in replacement of distribution transformers. 
(iv) In respect of other parameters, the Discoms disposed about more 
than 90% of the complaints of consumers, cases of 
reconnection, replacement of meters and release of new 
connections within the time-frame prescribed by OERC. 
As per available information, during January, 2007, there have been no 
notified power cuts on industry and agricultural consumers are being given 24 
hours supply in Orissa. 
(b) and (c) The Electricity Act, 2003 has provided for open access in 
transmision from the outset. The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission has 
already issued the enabling regulations for open access in inter-state transmission. 
This provision has created an all India market for electricity. 
The Act also provides for phased introduction of op en access in 
distribution by the State Electricity Regulatory Co mmissions. It provides that 
the SERC shall, not later than 27th January, 2009, by regulations, provide such 
open access to all consumers who require a supply o f electricity where the 
maximum power to be made available at any time exceeds one megawatt. Such 
a consumer would have the option to choose his supp liers other than the 
distribution licensee of his area. 
The Tariff Policy notified by the Central Governmen t provides that in 
whichever state the situation so permits, the Regul atory Commissions should 
introduce open access even prior to this deadline. The policy also lays down the 
methodology for computation of cross subsidy surcharge. 
14 

[26 February, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
According to the information available, the SERCs of 20 States have issued 
open access regulations in distribution and 17 SERCs have also specified the 
method of open access surcharge. 
The Electricity Act also provides for grant of license by the Appropriate 
Commission to two or more persons for distribution of electricity through their 
own distribution system within the same area, subject to compliance of additional 
requirements relating to the capital adequacy, cred itworthiness, or code of 
conduct prescribed by the Central Government. The additional requirements in 
this regard have also been notified.

7. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that literacy has to be integr al to any strategy for 
poverty alleviation as it is the single hurdle on the path to empowerment of the 
poor; 
(b) if so, the comments of Government thereon; 
(c) the aims and objectives set for the coming decade; 
(d) whether Government are making sustained efforts to cover every 
illiterate, gender-wise; and 
(e ) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) and 
(b) Literacy is integral to any strategy for poverty alleviation and plays a major 
role in the empowerment of the poor. The National Literacy Mission (NLM) aims 
to impart functional literacy to adult illiterates in the 15-35 age group. Functional 
Literacy, inter alia, implies:— 
• achieving self-reliance in literacy and numeracy 
• becoming aware of the causes of deprivation and mov ing towards 
amelioration of oppressive conditions through organ ization and 
participation in the process of development 
• acquisition of skilis to improve the economic status and general well-
being 
35 

RAJYA SABHA [26 February, 2007] 
The NLM recognizes that convergence of literacy programmes with the 
programmes of other development departments is esse ntial for the socio-
economic upliftmentof the beneficiaries. 
(c) to (e) At present, the combined efforts of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) 
and National Literacy Mission (NLM) aim at providing basic education to all persons 
in the 6-14 age-group and 15-35 age-group respectively. The goal of SSA is to 
universalize elementary education in the country. One of the main oojectives of 
SSA is to bridge all gender and social category gap s at primary stage by 2007 
and at elementary level by 2010. National Programme for Education of Girls at 
Elementary Level (NPEGEL) provides focused strategi es for girls in 
educationally backward blocks. Kasturba Gandhi Bali ka Vidyalayas are also 
provided in 1954 blocks aiming to provide residenti al facilities mainly for 
SC/ST/OBCs and girls belonging to minority communit ies to complete 
elementary education. 
The NLM seeks to impart functional literacy to adul t illiterates by 
providing basic literacy under the Total Literacy Campaigns, followed by Post 
Literacy Programme for reinforcement of literacy skills to the neo-literates and 
continuing education programme for providing opport unities for life-long 
education. So far, 597 districts in the country have been covered by the literacy 
programmes. Women learners constitute over 60% of the enrolment. 
It is envisaged that these efforts will be continue d during the next Plan 
with a greater focus on reducing the gender gap. Th e Approach Paper to the 
Eleventh Five Year Plan envisages increase in the l iteracy rate to 85%, 
substantial reduction in the drop-out rate of schoo l children and in the gender 
gap by the end of the Plan period

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (c) 
The National Programme of Nutritional Support to Pr imary Education (NP-
NSPE) was launched as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme on 15th August 1995, 
initially in 2408 blocks in the country. By the year 1997-98 the NP-NSPE was 
introduced in all blocks of the country. 
The NP-NSPE (commonly known as Mid-Day Meal Scheme) was 
48 

[26 February, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
extended in 2002 to cover children in classes l-V o f Government, 
Government Aided and local body schools, and also children studying in centres 
run under the Education Guarantee Scheme (EGS) and Alternative and Innovative 
Education (AIE) Scheme. 
Vide order dated 28.11.2001 passed in WP (C) 196/2001 the Supreme Court of 
India directed States to "implement the Mid Day meal Scheme by providing every 
child in every Government and Government assisted p rimary school with a 
prepared mid day meal with a minimum content of 300  CQlories and 8-12 
grams of protein each day of school for a minimum o f 200 days". Vide a 
subsequent order dated 24.4.2004 the Supreme Court of India directred that the 
Central Government shall provide the costs for conversion of foodgrains into a 
hot cooked meal. Accordingly, the NP-NSPE was revised in September 2004 to 
provide cooked med day meal with 300 calories and 8-12 grams of pr otein to 
all children studying in classes l-V in Government,  Government Aided 
schools and EGS/AIE centers, which cater to childre n from poor families as 
also SC and ST children. In addition to free supply of food grains, the schme also 
provided (a) colling cost @ Re 1 per child per school day, (b) transport subsidy 
at the rate of Rs. 100 per quintal for special category States, and Rs. 75 per quintal 
for other States, (c) management, monitoring and evaluation costs @ 2% of the 
cost of foodgrains, transport subsidy and cooking assistance, and (d) provision of 
mid day meal during summer vacation in drought affected areas. 
In July 2006 the Scheme was further revised to prov ide cooking cost at 
the enhanced rate of Rs. 21- per child per school day, of which the NER States 
were required to provide a minimum 20 paise per chi ld per school day, and 
non-NER States 50 paise per child per school day. T he nutritional norm was 
enhanced from 300 calories to 450 calories and prot ein content fixed at 12 
grams per child. In addition, the revised scheme pr ovides for construction of 
kitchen sheds and procurement of kitchen devices in  order to ensure that 
cooking is undertaken in safe and hygienic conditions.

foreign universities in arts, accountancy, medicine s and sciences, technical

countries of respective universities, institutions and/or academic councils 
awarding it;

According to the Association of Indian Universities (AIU), the Association has not 
accorded equivalence to the degrees awarded by any accredited foreign

63. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of MI NES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India has 8 per cent of the world's coal. 4 per 
cent of its iron ore and 7 per cent of its bauxite but so far India has surveyed its 
resources only by means of geological and seismic a nalysis and has not 
undertaken geo-physical and geo-chemical mapping to gauge what lies deep 
under the ground; and 
(b) if so, the steps Government propose to take to reform its outdated mining 
methods and tap the mineral resources in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF MINES (DR.  T 
SUBBARAMI REDDY): (a) As per Indian Bureau of Mines  (IBM), the 
percentage share of India's resources vis-a-vis world resources in respect of coal, 
iron ore and bauxite is about 27%, 7.65% and 10% re spectively. Geological 
Survey of India (GSI), which is the main agency of Government of India for 
survey and exploration of mineral resources, has employed airborne geophysical 
survey followed by ground checks of anomalous areas , ground geophysical 
exploration and sub surface drilling upto shallow level for exploring the mineral 
resources, GSI has initiated the programmes of National Geophysical Mapping in 
the Field Season 2002-03 and National Geochemical Mapping in Field Season 
2001-02. 
(b) GSI has inducted updated techniques for ground geophysical survey, 
precision analytical instruments and deep capacity drills and is in the process of 
acquiring heliborne survey system fitted with sensors for improving the quality 
of exploration and for tapping deep seated mineral resources. Mineral 
Exploration Corporation Limited (MECL), a public sector undertaking has also 
inducted remote sensing technique and sub surface g rophysical techniques for 
detailed exploration of mineral resources. Mining does not come under the purview 
of GSI and MECL. Government of India has opened up the mining sector to 
private entrepreneurs for attracting modern technol ogy for exploitation of 
mineral resources.

Steps for improvement in power distribution system  
81. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of PO WER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that power abundance and deprivation go together 
in the country as electricity surplus States are unable to light up their villages as 
they sell all they have, 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the country's power distribution system 
still suffers high aggregate technical and commerci al losses with a national 
average of 40 per cent; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take to impr ove the power 
distribution system in India? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHUKUMAR SHINDE): (a)  
Yes, Sir. Some of the States sell power to other St ates depending on the 
convenience and availability of short-term open access in the transmission system. 
Supply of electricity is a State subject as Section  6 of the Electricity Act, 
2003, provides that the State Government shall endeavour to supply electricity to 
all areas including villages and hamlets. 
(b) As per report prepared by Power Finance Corporation , Aggregate 
Technical and Commercial (AT&C) losses of the State  power distribution 
utilities at national level for the year 2004-05 were 33.82%. 
(c) Various steps taken by Government of India to reduce the losses of State 
Power Utilities and thereby improving the power distribution system are: 
(i) Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Progr amme 
(APDRP) was launched in 2002-03 under which Additio nal 
Central Assistance was provided to States for takin g up technical 
and commercial measures for strengthening and upgra dation of 
distribution network, improvement in billing and 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [26 February, 2007] 
collection efficiency, reduction in theft and improvement in 
consumer services etc. 
(ii) Electricity Act, 2003 has been enacted to brin g competition in the 
sector. It also provides legal framework for making  theft of 
electricity as cognizable offence. 
(iii) The National Electricity Policy was notified by the Ministry in 
2005 after consultations with various stakeholders. It aims at laying 
guidelines for accelerated development of the power  sector, 
providing supply of electricity to all areas and protecting interests of 
consumers and other stakeholders. 
(iv) With an objective to propagate adoption of bes t practices in the 
distribution sector, Ministry has organized Nationa l level 
workshops on best practices in distribution sector. 
(v) Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana (RGGVY ) is under 
implementation since April, 2005 to provide rural e lectricity 
infrastructure, which includes— 
1. Rural Electricity Distribution Backbone (REDB) with at least one 
33/11KV (or 66/11KV) sub-station in each block. 
2. Village Electrification Infrastructure (VEI) with at least one 
distribution transformer in each village/habitation. 
3. Decentralized Distributed Generation (DDG) Systems where grid 
supply is not feasible or cost-effective. 
This infrastructure so created will strengthen the distribution system and 
will reduce technical losses. Besides this the sche me provides for mandatory 
installation of franchisee system for rural distrib ution management to ensure 
revenue sustainability. This will reduce AT & C los ses. It has already started 
showing the results.

125 

RAJYA SABHA [26 February, 2007] 
Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) issued a s taff consultation paper 
on Developing a Common Platform for Electricity Trading inviting comments 
from the stakeholders. Subsequently, the CERC held a public hearing on the 
issue on 19th December, 2006 at New Delhi. 
After taking into account the comments received on the consultation paper 
and the deliberations held in the hearing on 19th D ecember, 2006, the CERC 
issued an Order dated 6.2.2007 stipulating the Guidelines for setting up of such 
Exchanges. The Guidelines lay down the procedure for making applications to 
CERC for establishing and operating such Exchanges, and related issues. Salient 
features of the guidelines are given in the Statement (See below). 
(c) The Power Exchange is aimed at better resource optimization for the 
power sector, generating strong investment signals making power trading 
transparent and efficient and safeguarding consumer interest. 
Statement  
Salient features of the CERC Guidelines for Setting Up of Power  
Exchange  
/head2right The general approach of the CERC is to allow operat ional freedom to 
the Power Exchange within an overall regulatory framework, 
/head2right Private entrepreneurship would be allowed to play i ts role. The CERC 
shall keep distance from governance of Power Exchange. 
/head2right The participation in the Power Exchange would be vo luntary and no 
existing Power Purchase Agreements and bilateral co ntracts would be 
disturbed. The CERC seeks to encourage Power Exchan ge to emerge as a 
market based institution for providing price discov ery and price risk 
management to the generators, distribution licensees, traders, consumers and 
other stake holders. The promoters shall be required to develop their own 
model Power Exchange and seek permission from the CERC before start of 
operation. The CERC has issued the following broad guidelines for 
developing of Power Exchange viz: 
126 

[26 February, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
• De-mutualized form of organisation 
• Reliable, effective and impartial management 
• Ring-fencing between ownership, management and participation 
• Investment support from the investors including ins titutional 
investors 
• Transparency in operation and decision-making 
• Computerized trading and clearing system 
• Efficient financial settlement and guarantee system 
• Effective trade information dissemination system 
/head2right The promoters will have the freedom to develop, man age 
and operate the Power Exchange according to approve d 
rules, bye-laws and procedures. The CERC will be co ncerned 
with the following aspects while granting permissio n to the 
Power Exchange: 
• Scrutiny of the Rules and bye-laws of the Power Exchange 
• Assignment of transmission capacity to the Power Exchange 
• Apportionment of transmission charges and losses 
• Procedure for handling transmission congestion. 
• Monitoring of the functioning of the Power Exchange  to the 
extent of preventing speculation, collusion and unfair gaming. 
• Adjudication of disputes between the Power Exchang e and 
.   the Members 
/head2right Any company registered under the Companies Act 6r a 
consortium of companies would be eligible for apply ing for 
setting up of the Power Exchange. The applicant wou ld be 
required to have adequate knowledge and understanding of the 
Indian Electricity Grid Code, Open Access Issues, Availability 
Based Tariff, Ul Mechanism, Scheduling Despatch and Energy 
Accounting Procedure. 
/head2right The applicant would be required to submit the follo wing 
details: 
127 

RAJYA SABHA [26 February, 2007] 
• Memorandum and Articles 01 Association of the compa ny 
making the application. 
• In case of a consortium, it should submit formal agreement among 
its Members, which should dwell upon the issues critical to the setting 
up of the Power Exchange. 
• Details of the existing business of the applicant company. 
• Net worth as defined under the Companies Act, 1956 of the 
applicant as on 1 st April of the financial year in  which the 
application is made in case of the companies formed prior thereto 
or on the date of making application in other cases. 
• Copies of the Annual Report and/or audited accounts  of the 
applicant for the last three years, to the extent t hese are 
applicable.    . 
• A project Report containing the following details: ' 
(i) Constitution of the proposed Power Exchange 
(ii) Funding sources of the proposed Power Exchange 
(iii) Management and Administrative structure of the proposed 
Power Exchange 
(iv) Infrastructural facilities available/proposed to be acquired by 
the Power Exchange. 
(v) Clearing and Settlement mechanism 
(vi). R&D facilities and training programmes likely to be made 
available by the proposed Power-Exchange 
• Rules and Bye-laws of the proposed Power Exchange 
/head2right The salient details of the applicant, proposed trading platform and 
website address where the full application is accessible shall be 
published in all editions of at least two national daily newspapers 
including one economic daily newspaper within 7 days of filing 
application inviting public comments/objections, if any upto a 
period of 30 days. 
128 

[26 February, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
/head2right The Commission, after making such inquiries as may be necessary 
in this behalf and after obtaining further informat ion as it may 
require, may grant permission for setting up of Pow er Exchange if 
it is satisfied in respect of the following:— 
• The rules and the bye-laws of the proposed Power Exchange are in 
conformity with such conditions as may be specified  by the 
Commission with a view to ensuring fair dealing and  to protect 
the interest of the stakeholders; 
• The rules and the bye-laws of the proposed Power Exchange do not, 
in any manner, violate the provisions of the Electr icity Act, 
2003, and the Rules and Regulations made there unde r and the 
provisions of Forward Contract Regulation Act, 1952; 
• The proposed Power Exchange is willing to comply wi th any 
other conditions, which the Commission may impose f or the 
purpose of carrying out the objects of the Electricity Act, 2003; 
• It would be in the interest of development of the electricity sector and 
also in the public interest to grant permission to the proposed 
Power Exchange. 
 
/head2right Before the permission is granted, the applicant shall be required to get the 
company registered as a Limited company under the C ompanies. Act, 
1966 exclusively for the purpose of Power Exchange. 
/head2right The CERC may withdraw permission granted to the Pow er Exchange 
after giving an opportunity of being heard, if it is satisfied that the functioning 
of the Power Exchange is in violation of the terms and conditions of 
permission, the bye-laws of the Power Exchange, the  provisions of the 
Electricity Act, 2003.

Interest of the young in science  
103. SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Will the Minister of SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in the backdrop of the Prime Minister expressing concern over 
declining interest of the young in science, the Ministry proposes an ambitious 
five-year scheme which incorporates measures such a s scholarship, summer 
camps with science icons and assured income for the talented in science to that 
they take up research as a career; 
(b) the details of the proposed scheme; and 
(c) by when it is likely to be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL 
SIBAL) (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) A special Scheme for Promoting Innovation in Science Pursuit 
for Inspired Research (INSPIRE), has been proposed by Department of Science and 
Technology, Ministry of Science and Technology, Gov ernment of India. The 
details of the proposed scheme along with the imple mentation schedule are 
given below. 
150 

[26 February, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
Motivation:  
There has been a felt need to strengthen the innovation infrastructure of India 
in her preparation for leveraging the enormous opportunities being offered by 
knowledge economies of the world. If Vision 2020 of  India to emerge a major 
knowledge and giobal power were to be realized, sufficient supply of young talents 
need to be attracted to study and take up careers with science. It is required that 
suitable systems and mechanisms to meet the innovat ive infrastructural needs 
for application of technology for wealth generation in the knowledge economy 
of 2020 be designed and implemented now. Advance actions with a foresight for 
building innovative knowledge infrastructure are being considered and proposed by 
the Ministry of Science and Technology. The motivation behind the proposed 
scheme "Innovation in Science Pursuit for inspired Research (INSPIRE)" is to prepare 
the Indian science and technology for a possible leadership position in 2020. 
Talent supply chain management: An essential need for converting 
comparative advantages into competitive strength:  
Currently, vast pool of talent supply is drawn more  effectively by 
service sectors in a competitive market environment  where management of 
technology plays a critical role. Generation of pre-competitive technology-based on 
first principles in science would form the differen tiating element in the 
knowledge based economies. In this endeavour, Human  Resource and talent 
supply chain management practices form the most cri tical component. India 
enjoys a natural comparative advantage by virtue of  demography and 
inherited knowledge systems. The conversion of comp arative advantage to 
competitive strength will require carefully planned interventions in a competitive 
world. 
Other major countries in Asia namely Japan, China and South Korea are 
deploying large financial resources and building their R&D infrastructure by scale 
expanding their doctoral research programs. It is e stiamted that China has 
multiplied the number of scholars undertaking Ph. D. studies in science by ten-
fold during the last fifteen years. An India specif ic model of conversion of 
comparative strength into competitive advantage calls for a suitable scheme to 
offer for young people with both aptitude and talen t careers with science and 
innovation as a choice. INSPIRE is a proposed innovation to offer science as an 
carrer option by providing necessary 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [26 February, 2007] 
opportunities for youth with aptitude for careers seeking innovation and psychic delight in 
addition to reasonable physical income. 
Features of the proposed scheme "INSPIRE":  
The scheme proposed inspire includes three elements in different age groups. 
They are (a) providing Science innovation scholarship of Rs. 5000 for a total of one 
million young learners of the age group 10-17 once in their school career during the next 
five years for experiencing the joy of innovations(b) providing a mentorship through global 
icons including 60-70 Nobel prize winners and 150-200 Indian leaders in science through a 
summer camp for the top 1% performers in the Class X examination every year for a 
period of five years and (c) offering scholarship for doctoral research backed by an assured 
research carrer opportunity scheme for a total of 1000 young people leaving plus two level 
for a period of five years after their Ph. D. in sciences. This integrated approach provides a 
hand holding and safety net mechanism for identifying and nurturing youth with aptitude and 
talent for research. Unless the nation nourishes the root of innovation, it will find it difficult 
to bear the fruit. The model of China based on quantum increases in R & D base and supply 
of funds may be difficult to bear the fruit. The model of China based on quantum 
increases in R&D base and supply of funds may be difficult for India to match. India 
model is therefore based on identifying early and building the required human resource 
base for the country within the absorption capacity of our current S & T system and 
R&D base. Estimated fund requirements for 2007-2012:  
The proposed scheme INSPIRE estimates the fund requirement of about Rs 1500 
crores for a period of five years with a break up is given below:

(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. The reports bring out a need for improved delivery of 
services and infrastructure facilities. The concerned State Governments have been 
asked to improve the infrastructure facilities and upscale the delivery and quality 
of services so that ICDS scheme achieves its objective to reduce mainutrition 
among children. States have been requested to take appropriate corrective 
measures. 
(d) An appraisal of three decades of ICDS has been conducted by 
National Institute of Public Cooperation and Child Development in 2006. 
The study covered 150 ICDS Projects from 35 States/ UTs covering rural, 
urban and tribal projects. A total of five Anganwad i Centres (AWCs) were 
randomly selected from each sample project covering  750 AWCs. The 
main findings of the appraisal is as under: 
(i) Around 59 per cent AWCs studied have no toilet facility and in 17 
per cent this facility was found to be unsatisfactory; 
(ii) Around 75% of AWCs have pucca buildings, 
(iii) 44 per cent AWCs covered under the study were  found to be 
lacking in PSE kits; 
(iv) Disruption of supplementary nutrition was noticed on an average of 
46.31 days at Anganwadi level. Major reason causing  disruption 
was reported as delay in supply of items of supplem entary 
nutrition; 
(v) 35.5 per cent mothers did not report weighing o f new born 
children; 
(vi) 29 per cent children were born with a low birth weight which was 
below normal (less than 2500 gm); 
(vii) 37 per cent AWWs reported non-availability of materials/ aids for 
Nutrition and Health Education (NHED). 
(e) Recently, to strengthen the existing monitoring  and supervision 
mechanism for ICDS Scheme, the Government of India has approved setting 
up of a Central Monitoring Unit (CMU) at National I nstitute of Public 
Cooperation and Child Development (NIPCCD), which w ould monitor the 
Scheme through independent professional organizatio n/institution in each 
State/UT. This would be in addition to the monitori ng mechanism in place

identify SC and ST hamlets/habitations for setting up AWCs and also to ensure

left out.

The Ministry of Women and Child Development has formulated a scheme named 
Integrated Child Protection Scheme (ICPS) largely for children upto eighteen years 
of age. The Working Group on Development of Children for the 11th Plan has also 
recommended this scheme. The aim of this scheme is to institutionalize essential 
services and strengthen structures, enhance capacities at all levels, create data

State Child Protection Units (SCPUs) and District Child Protection Units (DCPUs) 
through the State Governments.

Dissatisfaction on ICDS 
125. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT:Will the Minister of WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Hon'ble Prime Ministe r has expressed 
dissatisfaction on the implementation of Integrated  Children Development 
Scheme; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken to have this scheme properly 
implemented for the benefit of maximum number of eligible children. 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and 
(b) The Hon'ble Prime Minister has expressed concern over the current status of 
implementation of the ICDS Scheme. A number of Repo rts and Surveys, 
including the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-3) and Focus on Children 
Under Six (FOCUS) have indicated a decline in the q ualitative aspects of the 
programme in some of the States/UTs. 
(c) The Hon'ble Prime Minister has impressed upon t he States to 
adequately empower the Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) and Urban Local 
Bodies (ULBs) to monitor and supervise the Anganwadi Centres and to make line 
officials accountable. Taking cognizance of the Pri me Minister's 
observations, the Ministry of Women and Child Devel opment has set up a 
National Level Monitoring Committee under the Chairpersonship of MOS (WCD) to 
oversee the entire functioning of ICDS Scheme and to ensure that the services 
are delivered to the target groups in an effective manner and the objectives of the 
scheme are fulfilled. Apart from this, the Government of India has also set up a 
Central Monitoring Unit (CMU) at National Institute of Public Cooperation and 
Child Development (NIPCCD) which would monitor the Scheme through 
independent professional organization/institution in each State/UT This would 
be in addition to the monitoring mechanism in place at present. 
To achieve universalization of ICDS and maximize th e coverage of 
beneficiaries, further relaxation of the population  norms has been 
recommended by Inter-Ministerial Task Force. Action for further expansion of 
ICDS Scheme would be initiated, after the approval of the Report of the Task 
Force by the competent authority.

Report on malnutrition of children 
126. SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether according to a report released globally by the Washington based 
International Good Policy Institute, India ranks 3rd from the bottom of the world 
on malnourished kids; 
(b) if so, the other main points mentioned in the report; and 
(c) the steps Government propose to take in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) The 
International Food Policy Research Institute, Washi ngton has published the 
Global Hunger Index (GHI), capturing 3 dimensions o f hunger; insufficient 
availability of food, shortfalls in the nutritional  status of children and child 
mortality. In the Index, information available from the reports of FAO 2005, WHO 
2006 and UNICEF 2005 has been used. India ranks 96th in the said GHI out of 
119 developing countries. 
(b) The main points mentioned in the said report are: 
(i) Sub Saharan Africa and South Asia are hot spots  of hunger and 
undernutrition. However, positive trends can also be observed throughout 
most of South and Southeast Asia, particularly in India and China. 
(ii) India's current score of 25.73 is an improveme nt on its 
performance of 41.23 since the first index was published in 1981. 
(iii) China and India, the population giants in East Asia and South Asia, 
made large contributions to the overall very positive trends in these 
two regions: 
• Cereal yields more than doubled in India between 1961— 1997 
• The proportion of undernourished was reduced in the country 
• Access to safe water increased notably by the 1990s (from 54 per 
cent to 81 per cent) 
188 

[26 February, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
• Per capita Gross National Income more than doubled in India 
from 1980 to 2003 
• Underweight in children was reduced by more than 20  
percentage points in India 
• Under-5 Mortality rate was halved in India from 198 1 to 
2003. 
(c) The Government is already seized of the problem  and is 
implementing a number of schemes to improve the nut ritional status of 
children. Some of these are as under: 
(i) Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) (M instry of 
Women and Child Development); 
(ii) National Programme for Nutritional Support to Primary 
Education (Mid Day Meal Scheme) (Department of Scho ol 
Education and Literacy); 
(iii) Nutrition Programme for Adolescent Girls in 5 1 districts to 
provide free foodgrains to undernourished adolescent girls and 
pregnant and nursing mothers (Ministry of Women and  Child 
Development); 
(iv) Nutrition Education and Training Programmes of  Food and 
Nutrition Board (Ministry of Women and Child 
Development); 
(v) National Rural Health Mission including deliver y of Iron and 
Folic Acid and Vitamin A Supplementation programmes  and 
Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Ill nesses 
(Ministry of Health and Family Welfare); 
(vi) National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control P rogramme 
(Ministry of Health and Family Welfare); 
(vii) Targetted Public Distribution System (Department of Food and 
Public Distribution). 
(viii) Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme/Swa jaldhara and 
Total Sanitation Campaign; National Rural Employmen t 
Guarantee Programme (Ministry of Rural Development).
